---
title: "Decisions and Backstories"
---


Every entry here has the same shape: the situation, the options that were real,
the choice, and what the choice cost. Entries marked **[ops]** are operational
practice from the operator's engineering notes; the repository cannot corroborate
them, and they are labelled so a reader can tell the difference.

## 1. Local-first, and what that forbids {#sec-dec-local}

**Situation.** Mainstream assistants in this category are cloud products with
large dependency surfaces. The author wanted an assistant that runs on one machine
and can be understood end to end.

**Options considered.** (a) Extend a general framework; (b) keep the dependency
list small and support local model servers only; (c) local-first with hosted
escape hatches where they are genuinely better.

**Choice.** (c), with a strong bias toward (b). The provider registry supports
four kinds — three local, one "any OpenAI-compatible endpoint" — and nothing
requires an account. Web search and speech-to-text may use hosted providers, but
both degrade to a warning when unconfigured.

**Cost.** Features that assume a strong hosted model are simply absent. Reasoning
effort is opt-in because not every local model supports it. The `image` provider
role exists because a text-only main model cannot read a screenshot.

## 2. Fork, then diverge {#sec-dec-fork}

**Situation.** Build a personal assistant. Write one from scratch, or start from
something that already works?

**Choice.** Fork an existing minimal Python agent and keep its skeleton — bus,
loop, tools — while growing a different architecture around it.

**Why.** The fork's shape is genuinely good for this problem: a message bus, a
tool loop, a provider layer. There was no reason to rewrite those. Everything the
project is actually *about* — channels, sessions, memory, scheduling, a web UI, a
job ledger — did not exist in the starting point and now constitutes most of the
code.

**Cost.** Over 878 commits the divergence is total: the channel layer, session
management, the gateway lifecycle, the dashboard and the backend trigger path are
all new. The fork is now ancestry rather than architecture. What remains of the
original is the shape of the turn loop and the module layout, both of which have
been heavily extended.

## 3. One process, one event loop {#sec-dec-process}

**Situation.** The system needs a web dashboard, a chat bot, a scheduler, an IMAP
poller and a model client. Each could be its own process.

**Options considered.** (a) Multi-process with IPC; (b) one process with threads;
(c) one asyncio process hosting everything, including the HTTP servers.

**Choice.** (c).

**Why it works.** The dashboard's `aiohttp` app and the backend channel's app run
*inside the gateway's event loop*. There is no serialisation between the web
request that starts a turn and the turn itself: the request handler publishes an
`InboundMessage` and returns. A websocket frame and a cron tick travel the same
path a Telegram update does. Threads are used in exactly one place — the skill
file watcher — and it hands work back to the loop through a queue.

**Cost.** One slow blocking call in the loop stalls everything. This is why the
heavy model listing and context-length detection run in a thread or behind short
timeouts, and why the reviewer is gated on model idleness instead of running
concurrently.

## 4. Channels as adapters over a two-dataclass bus {#sec-dec-bus}

**Situation.** Five very different integrations need to reach the same agent.

**Rejected first.** Giving the agent a channel-specific entry point, or inventing
a richer event hierarchy per channel.

**Choice.** Two dataclasses and two queues. `InboundMessage` and
`OutboundMessage`, with a free-form `metadata` dict on both.

**Why.** The bus stays two concepts wide forever. Anything new a channel needs —
thread identifiers, image roles, progress flags, side-conversation markers —
travels in `metadata` instead of widening the bus. Session identity is a property
computed on the message, so every downstream subsystem agrees on it for free.

**Cost.** `metadata` is untyped, and the consequences of that are handled by
convention: keys are underscore-prefixed for internal markers, and every consumer
that reads one documents what it expects. A wrong key fails quietly. This is a
deliberate trade of static safety for extensibility in a system with exactly one
integrator.

## 5. A SQLite knowledge base instead of markdown-only memory {#sec-dec-kb}

**[ops]** This decision lives in the operator's workspace tooling, not in the
package, so it is described as practice.

**Situation.** Markdown memory files are pleasant to read and edit by hand, but
they stop working as a knowledge base past a few hundred facts: recall is
substring matching, everything is in every prompt, and consolidation turns into
guesswork about what to merge.

**Choice.** Durable facts live in a SQLite database with full-text search, behind
a small command-line interface. The Markdown memory files are demoted to *indexes*
— short, human-readable pointers into the database — rather than being the store.

**Why.** Search becomes a query instead of a grep, dedup becomes
search-then-update instead of eyeballing, and the index files stay small enough to
be injected into a prompt without cost. The single-writer discipline that follows
from a CLI is the point: every durable fact enters through one path, so there is
no question about who wrote what or when.

**Cost.** A fact that is not in the database does not exist, including for the
operator. The CLI is a hard dependency of the workflow, and the index files drift
if they are edited by hand — which is exactly why they are treated as generated.

## 6. Idle-time review instead of a background thread per session {#sec-dec-review}

**Situation.** The agent should learn durable facts from conversations. Commit
`9046c87` records the earlier design: three writers — a per-message suggestion
hook, a periodic consolidation pass, and a periodic archival pass — all writing the
same memory file, producing duplicate entries and lost writes.

**Choices.** (a) Fix the races; (b) keep one writer but run it concurrently;
(c) keep one writer and run it only when the model is idle.

**Choice.** (c), and the reviewer refuses to start while any model call is in
flight.

**Why.** The concurrency is not the interesting constraint — the *hardware* is.
Two simultaneous calls to a local model server halve throughput for the user's
own conversation. Idle-time review costs the user nothing and still runs after
every turn.

**Crash safety.** The compromise this creates is that a session can be archived
before its review finished. That is handled explicitly rather than ignored: the
archive is stamped `archived: false`, a one-shot sweep at gateway startup
re-processes anything still unstamped and then flips the stamp, and the archive
pruner refuses to delete unstamped files. Learning is at-least-once, and the
dedup check before each write makes that safe.

## 7. watchdog over watchfiles {#sec-dec-watchdog}

**Situation.** Skills must hot-reload without a restart.

**Choice.** `watchdog`'s `Observer` with a custom event handler, not
`watchfiles`.

**Why.** The handler receives raw filesystem events, which makes two things easy
that would otherwise need extra machinery: filtering to `SKILL.md` only, and
debouncing per path. The handler runs on a watchdog thread and does nothing but
push `(event_type, path)` onto an `asyncio.Queue`; all mutation happens on the
event loop, so the registry is never touched from two threads. It is also a pure
Python package with no native wheel to build, which matters for a tool whose
whole premise is "install it and it works".

**Cost.** The debounce window is a hand-rolled one-second timer rather than a
library feature, and the observer's lifecycle has to be managed explicitly on
start and stop.

## 8. A compact skills summary instead of inlined skills {#sec-dec-skillprompt}

**Situation.** Skills are Markdown documents. Inlining them all into the system
prompt would be expensive and would blow the context on a small local model.

**Choice.** Generate a compact summary — category, count, availability, member
names — and let the agent read the full `SKILL.md` with the file tool when it
decides the skill applies.

**Why.** Skill *discovery* becomes cheap and constant-size, while skill *content*
is paid for only when used. Availability is computed from each skill's declared
requirements so the summary tells the model what is actually runnable on this
machine, not merely what is installed.

**Cost.** The agent has to make a decision to spend a tool call. A skill with a
weak name or description simply never gets read; the summary line is therefore the
most important text in the file, not the body.

## 9. Session epochs: cost accounting that survives "start a new chat" {#sec-dec-epoch}

**Situation.** Usage is recorded per session key. But a session key is reused
across the whole life of a chat, so "how much has this conversation cost?" grows
without bound and `/new` does not reset it.

**Choice.** Add an epoch counter, persisted per session key. Every usage row
carries the epoch that was current when it was recorded, and a new conversation
advances the epoch.

**Why.** Cost can then be reported per *conversation* rather than per *key*, with
no destructive deletion of history — the ledger stays append-only and the
`usage_sessions` table holds the authoritative current epoch, so a crash between
"advance" and "next turn" cannot desynchronise. The footer shows the session cost
at the current epoch.

**Cost.** One more dimension in every usage query and one more migration step
(schema version 3). The epoch is resolved once per turn, not per record, so the
hot path stays cheap.

## 10. The 500-message cap and what a long-lived cron session did about it {#sec-dec-cron-cap}

**Situation.** Sessions are trimmed to a configurable cap — 500 messages by
default — when saved to disk. Cron jobs reuse a *stable* per-job key, so their
session is truncated forever and never grows past the rotation threshold.

**The failure.** Because the trim kept the file at the cap, the rotation check
never fired. The session was reused indefinitely on a rolling window of stale
context until a run's prompt blew past the model's context, at which point the run
silently produced nothing and *still reported success*. Commit `67a3176` records
the fix and the reasoning.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-rotation
%%| fig-cap: "Rotation policy after the fix. Interactive sessions may rotate mid-turn; cron sessions rotate only between runs, so a run in progress is never interrupted."
flowchart TB
  ADD["add_message()"] --> Q1{"interactive<br/>session?"}
  Q1 -->|yes| R1{"messages >=<br/>rotation cap?"}
  R1 -->|yes| ARC["archive + fresh session"]
  R1 -->|no| KEEP["append"]
  Q1 -->|no| KEEP
  GOC["get_or_create()<br/>between turns"] --> Q2{"cron session?"}
  Q2 -->|yes| R2{"messages ><br/>trim cap?"}
  R2 -->|yes| ARC
  R2 -->|no| KEEP
  Q2 -->|no| R3{"messages >=<br/>rotation cap?"}
  R3 -->|yes| ARC
  R3 -->|no| KEEP
  style ARC fill:#eaf3ec,stroke:#5f8a6d
```

**The rule that came out of it.**

- Cron sessions never rotate mid-turn — a rotation in the middle of a run would
  destroy the run's context.
- Cron sessions rotate *between* runs, at the trim cap, on both the cached path and
  the cold-load path (a session loaded from disk after a restart may already be
  over the threshold).
- Cron sessions are exempt from the save-time trim, with a generous safety cap
  instead, so the archive captures their full history rather than a rolling
  window.
- Archives get an explicit retention policy, because nothing else reaps them.

**The generalisable lesson.** A cap and a rotation threshold are different
numbers. When a trim keeps a value below the threshold that triggers rotation, the
rotation is dead code that nobody notices until the context explodes.

## 11. The scheduler caches jobs in memory, so restart discipline became a rule {#sec-dec-cron-cache}

**Situation.** The scheduler reads its job file once at startup and keeps the job
list in memory, re-saving the file on every mutation.

**The failure.** Editing the job file from outside — by hand, or with a script
that was not the scheduler — is silently undone. The next save writes the
in-memory copy back over the edit. Nothing errors; the change simply disappears.

**Choice.** Keep the cache. It is the right structure: one owner for the job list,
no read-modify-write races between the CLI and the timer, no file locking.

**The price, paid explicitly.** Editing scheduler state is now an operation that
requires a gateway restart to take effect, so that fact became a documented
operational rule rather than a trap:

| Change | Takes effect | Action |
|--------|--------------|--------|
| Model, provider, temperature, reasoning effort | Next turn | Nothing — hot-reloaded by mtime check |
| Skill file | Immediately | Nothing — file watcher |
| Workspace file or memory | Next turn | Nothing |
| Cron job file | **After restart** | Restart the gateway |
| Gateway source | **After restart** | Redeploy script, then restart |

**Lesson.** Caching in-memory is almost always the right call; the mistake is
failing to write down which caches exist. Here the cache is the reason the
restart rule exists, and the rule is now a table rather than folklore.

## 12. The backend channel: a third trigger path {#sec-dec-backend}

**Situation.** Originally there were two ways to start a turn: a human in a chat,
or a schedule. Both are person-shaped. Automated work — a long-running job, a
worker, a migration — has nobody to press the button.

**Choice.** A channel adapter that is not a chat platform at all. It accepts
signed event envelopes on a loopback endpoint and tails the jobs database for new
events, and each event wakes an isolated session scoped to its job.

**Why an adapter, not a hook.** Because an adapter gets session isolation, the
message bus, usage accounting, the agent loop, and reply handling for free. A hook
would have to reimplement all of it, badly.

**Why two ways in.** Pushing over HTTP is simple and immediate, and a producer may
not have a database. Tailing the database needs no producer changes at all: a job
that already writes events gets woken for free. The tailer stores a high-watermark
and starts *after* existing rows, so enabling it never replays history into a
session.

**Security posture.** Refuses to start without a credential, forces a non-loopback
bind address back to loopback, compares credentials in constant time, and opens the
jobs database read-only.

**Cost.** Replies have nowhere to go. They are logged, unless the envelope names a
channel to escalate to — which is the one case where a machine-initiated turn is
allowed to interrupt a human.

## 13. Jobs are a ledger, not a log file {#sec-dec-jobsdb}

**[ops]** The job tooling is workspace-side; the *consumers* are in the package.

**Situation.** Long-running delegated work needs to be observable: what is
running, what is stuck, what finished, and what did it actually produce.

**Rejected.** Parsing the agent's log output.

**Choice.** One SQLite database with a jobs table (status enum, repo, model, spec
and result paths, timestamps) and a `job_events` table forming the timeline.

**Why.** A status enum is queryable; a log line is not. A structured event table
supports "show me everything that happened to this job in order" with one indexed
query, which is exactly what the dashboard's detail view does. And because the
events are rows, the backend tailer can select on them.

**Completion detection is a file, not a pattern match.** The producer writes a
done-marker file when the work is genuinely finished. Nothing greps a log for a
success phrase. Grepping logs is fragile in a way that is invisible until it
matters: log rotation truncates the evidence, concurrent runs interleave, and a
model quoting the phrase it was looking for produces a false positive. A file's
existence is a contract that cannot be misread.

## 14. Dashboard parity means behaviour *and* confirmation {#sec-dec-parity}

**Situation.** The dashboard is supposed to be "the same assistant, in a browser".
The first attempts implemented the *mechanism* — an endpoint that starts a new
session — and still did not match.

**The chain of commits is the story:**

1. `0138361` — make the dashboard's "new chat" archive the session the way
   Telegram's `/new` does. Mechanism parity.
2. `cade0bc` — persist the rotation to disk, fix the mobile layout and the PWA
   cache headers.
3. `9d9747c` — fix the subtle one: the new-chat path was archiving a *stale disk
   copy* of the session, because the live conversation only lives in memory and is
   flushed opportunistically. Every message since the last save was silently
   dropped from the archive. The fix archives the cached session when there is one.
4. `9d535f2` — add the success toast, so the user is told "session archived, new
   chat started".

**The rule.** Parity is behaviour *plus* confirmation UX. A feature that works but
does not say it happened is not done. The user must not have to open the
transcript to find out whether something was saved.

## 15. Per-session concurrency instead of one global dispatch lock {#sec-dec-concurrency}

**Situation.** A single lock around message dispatch meant one slow turn blocked
every other conversation — including `/btw` side questions and background work.

**Choice.** Three layers, in a fixed order: a global lock for runtime hot-reload
and config mutation, a semaphore capping concurrent sessions, then a per-session
lock. Commit `5929cc3` and its tests cover cross-session parallelism, ordering
within a session, registry cleanup when locks go idle, `/stop` isolation, and the
global cap.

**Why a lock *registry* rather than a single lock.** Sessions are created and
destroyed constantly; a fixed set of locks would leak. The registry creates a lock
on first use and drops it when it is unlocked with no waiters, which is why the
tests assert the registry does not grow.

**Why the lock ordering is documented.** Deadlock avoidance by convention is
fragile. The rule — global before session, never the reverse — is written at the
point of acquisition where it would be violated, and the concurrency tests are
what keep the convention honest.

**The same commit added guards elsewhere** for the same reason: an `asyncio.Lock`
around memory writes, the scheduler's job list, and the subagent task registry.
The lesson is that per-session concurrency does not remove the need for locking;
it moves it to the objects that are actually shared.

## 16. Restart: script for source, CLI for configuration {#sec-dec-restart}

**Situation.** After landing a change to the gateway, the running process still
has the old code. Something has to restart it.

**Choices.** (a) Kill by pattern; (b) restart by hand; (c) a redeploy script for
source and a CLI restart for configuration.

**Choice.** (c). The redeploy script reinstalls the package, writes a
restart-request flag containing where to send the confirmation, restarts the
daemon through its own CLI, and lets the new process consume the flag and send a
boot notification reporting version and provider status. Configuration-only
changes use the CLI restart command.

**The incident that produced the rule.** An ad-hoc `kill` by process-name pattern
was run from inside a session. The pattern matched the shell command that was
running the kill, so the session killed itself. Recovery took roughly eight
minutes. The rule is now blunt: **restart through the CLI, never by hand.**

**Why the flag file exists at all.** Because a restart is asynchronous from the
operator's point of view. Writing "please tell me when you're back" to disk before
restarting is what turns a silent restart into an observable one — and it is why
the confirmation includes the version that is now live, which is what
[versioning](#sec-dec-versioning) depends on.

## 17. Versioning: the deploy log is the source of truth {#sec-dec-versioning}

**[ops]**

**Situation.** With an editable install and a restart-based deploy, "which code is
running?" becomes a real question, not a rhetorical one.

**Choice.** Semantic version bumps committed alongside the change, a deploy log
recording each deployed version, commit messages that reference the unit of work,
and a boot notification that reports the version of the running process.

**Why.** The running process reports its own version at boot, and the deploy log
records what was pushed when. Together they answer "is the fix live?" without
anyone having to remember. Referencing the work unit in the commit message is what
makes the history navigable: `git log --grep` finds every change belonging to a
decision, and the Engineering Log at the end of this book is written from exactly
that history.

**Cost.** Version discipline is manual. It is kept honest by bumping in the same
commit as the behaviour change, never in a batch.

## 18. Tests, and treating a green suite as a claim {#sec-dec-testing}

**Situation.** A single-operator project still accumulates enough moving parts —
a scheduler, a watcher, three HTTP servers, four databases — that regressions are
guaranteed without tests.

**Choice.** `unittest`-style suites under `tests/`, mandatory for every unit of
work, plus two pieces of hygiene that matter more than usual here:

- **Isolation by default.** An autouse fixture redirects the usage store to a
  per-test temporary database, so no test can write to the production ledger even
  if the test author forgets. The store has its own second net for the same
  reason.
- **A flaky test is a defect.** A suite that must be re-run to be believed is not
  green, it is noisy. The rule is: re-run before trusting green; if it fails
  again, record it and fix it.

**And the cultural half.** Incidents and corrections are written down as durable
facts, and the most important ones are promoted into the protected hard-lessons
region of memory so trimming can never drop them. The cap-and-protect design in
[Chapter 3](03-patterns.qmd#sec-pat-memory) exists because of this: the most
valuable thing in the memory file is the thing that must survive.

## What the decisions have in common {#sec-dec-common}

Read the list backwards and a single theme emerges: **the code is the cheap part,
the invariants are the expensive part.**

- Every cache in the system is documented as a cache, so "why did my edit vanish"
  is answerable.
- Every trimmer protects its most valuable content, because trimming is where
  value silently leaks.
- Every fan-out point — the bus, the API, the lock registry — has an invariant
  written at the point where it would be broken.
- Every capability that could be asynchronous but shouldn't, isn't: review waits
  for idleness, the scheduler waits for its timer, one agent per repository waits
  for the last one.

The through-line from Chapter 1 is intact. The requirement was that the data flow
be traceable. The decisions above are what it costs to keep that true as the system
grows.
